title: Flex Sizing
summary: Explains how a flex container works out the size of each flex item: a priority list of size sources, the min/max limits, and the flex-grow, flex-shrink and flex-basis properties with the flex shorthand. Ends with an online exercise where you reproduce the resize behaviour of a target flex container.

concepts.heading: Default behaviour of flex items
points: Paragraphs are normally full-width block elements. Once their parent is display: flex they become flex items laid out along the main axis (a row by default), each sized to its content with no gaps unless gap is set.
With no sizing properties at all, items already respond to window resizing: they shrink with the container down to a minimum size, then overflow off the page.

The default minimum size of an item is the width of its longest word (text will wrap but a word is not broken). The default ideal/maximum size is all of its text on one line. So the item with the longest single word stays widest when squeezed.

concepts.heading: Priority list used to pick an item's size
points: 1. min-width / max-width (or min-height / max-height in a column) act as hard limits and win over everything else.
2. flex-basis, if set. It sets the starting size along the main axis (width in a row, height in a column).
3. width (or height in a column container), if there is no flex-basis.
4. Otherwise the natural content size.
Because flex-basis outranks width, setting both is pointless: the width is ignored in a row container.

concepts.heading: width and flex-basis in practice
points: Setting width: 100px on each of four items gives four 100px boxes while the container is at least 400px wide (plus any gaps).
When the container gets narrower than the total, the items are still allowed to shrink (flex-shrink defaults to 1), but never below their minimum content size, so the longest word stays intact.
Setting flex-basis: 200px makes each item aim for 200px and overrides the width. It shrinks the same way once space runs out.

concepts.heading: max-width and min-width
points: max-width caps how large an item may become. If flex-basis is 200px but max-width is 100px, the item ends at 100px even with plenty of room. If flex-basis is smaller than max-width (e.g. 50px), the basis is used.
max-width therefore limits growth potential; items still shrink and grow with the container but only within the cap.
min-width sets how small an item may shrink. If min-width (300px) is larger than flex-basis (200px), the item renders at 300px and will not shrink below it.
Both properties replace the content-derived defaults if you set them explicitly, which is sometimes useful.

concepts.heading: flex-grow and flex-shrink
points: These provide the 'flexible' part of flexbox. flex-grow says whether an item may expand into spare space; flex-shrink says whether it may contract when space is short. Value 0 turns each off.
grow 0 and shrink 0: items stay fixed at the basis size whatever the window does. It stops behaving like a flexible layout.
grow 1 and shrink 0: items start at the basis, expand to fill the container when it widens, but do not shrink under the basis (they overflow instead).
grow 0 and shrink 1: this is the default for flex items. Items begin at their basis, do not stretch, but can shrink down to their minimum content width.
grow 1 and shrink 1: items expand to fill the container and also shrink; the basis is effectively just a starting point, and the limits come from max/min-width or content.
The default flex-basis is auto, which uses the width if set, else the content size, so items with more text get a bigger share. Setting flex-basis: 0 removes this and makes shares equal.

concepts.heading: The flex shorthand
points: flex: <grow> <shrink> <basis>, in that order, e.g. flex: 1 1 0.
A single unitless number such as flex: 1 means grow 1, shrink 1, basis 0, so every item gets an equal share.

Different numbers set proportions: an item with flex: 2 and another with flex: 1 split the space 2:1 and keep that ratio as the container is resized. This is how the earlier section's red/blue boxes with different flex values worked.

task.name: Match the resize behaviour of the green flex box
task.starting_point: An external exercise page with a CSS text box and an 'Apply CSS' button. A green flex container (the target) and a blue container (yours) hold three items. Target widths are listed on screen: item 1 200px, item 2 200px, item 3 400px.
task.goal: Write CSS so the blue container resizes exactly like the green one, which means matching both the static layout and the behaviour while the window is resized.
steps: Set justify-content: space-between on the container to match how the items are spread.
Give the items flex-basis values of 200px, 200px and 400px.
Resize the window and watch the green box: only item 1 shrinks, items 2 and 3 hold their size.
Set flex-shrink: 0 on item 2 and item 3, leaving item 1 on its default shrink of 1.
Press Apply CSS and re-test by resizing.
task.expected_result: Blue items look identical to the green ones at full width and respond identically when the window is narrowed.

pitfalls: Checking only the static layout: matching widths is not enough, you must resize to compare grow/shrink behaviour.
Setting width and flex-basis together; the width is ignored in a row container.
Expecting a flex-basis larger than max-width to win. The max-width limit wins.
Setting both grow and shrink to 0 and wondering why the layout no longer responds.
Leaving flex-basis on auto when you want equal item sizes; use flex: 1 (basis 0).
(Extra) The selectors in the solution are illustrative; the exercise page uses its own class names.

playground.coverage: That lesson's explore demo has sliders for flex-grow, flex-basis and a note on flex-shrink (default 1). Equal split and double share via grow values are explained.
gaps_and_ideas: Add a dedicated 'Flex sizing' lesson (9.2b) with the four-step priority list: min/max, flex-basis, width, content.
Add sliders/checkboxes for min-width, max-width and flex-shrink plus a draggable container width, so learners see items hit their limits.
Show the 'longest word' minimum size with a long-word paragraph to explain why items stop shrinking.
